title: The fifth
hook: in Shia law, a fifth of yearly surplus is also due, half for the Imam's share through scholars, half for needy descendants of the Prophet ﷺ

segments.voice: Yesterday, the eight, and your line: eight doors. Which door stayed with you, and did you give through it? Today, a second share, kept by Twelver Shia Muslims alongside zakat. Day one thousand one hundred one.

A family in a Shia home sits down on a set day of the year with a notebook. Not their zakat day; another one. They add up what came in over the year. They subtract what the year cost: rent, food, school, the car repair, the gifts for Eid. Whatever is left, the surplus, the money the year didn't need, they divide by five. One part of five is not theirs to keep. Some of it goes, through the office of a senior scholar they follow, to the work of religion. Some goes to needy families descended from the Prophet ﷺ. Today, the fifth: khums.
screen: `A NOTEBOOK, ONCE A YEAR.` → `WHAT CAME IN, MINUS WHAT IT COST.` → `ONE PART OF FIVE.`

segments.voice: First, the verse. Surah eight, verse forty-one, speaks of whatever you take as gains, and says a fifth of it belongs to Allah and the messenger, to the near kin, the orphans, the needy and the wayfarer. Both communities read the same verse. They read one of its words differently. Second, the Sunni reading. Sunni scholars read the verse about the spoils taken in war, a fifth of which was set aside for these purposes. They also apply a fifth to buried treasure that someone finds: a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says that on found treasure, the share is a fifth. Beyond those, Sunni law asks zakat, not khums, of ordinary savings. Third, the Shia reading. Twelver Shia scholars read the verse's word for gains broadly, as any gain, and they rely on reports from the Imams of the Prophet's family that apply it to a person's yearly profit. So in Twelver Shia law, a fifth of the year's surplus is due, after the year's real expenses, alongside zakat. Their jurists divide it in two. Half is the share of the Imam, which today is given through a senior scholar, a marja', to support religious learning and the community. Half is for needy descendants of the Prophet ﷺ, who in this teaching may not receive zakat from those outside the family. Fourth, what to notice, whichever reading you meet. Both start from the same verse. Both send the share to the near kin, the orphan, the needy and the traveler. The difference is in a word and in the scholars each community follows, and each gives its reasons. A friend who pays khums is following their law, as a friend who doesn't is following theirs.
screen: `ONE VERSE: A FIFTH OF GAINS.` · `SUNNI: SPOILS AND FOUND TREASURE.` · `SHIA: A FIFTH OF YEARLY SURPLUS.` · `ONE VERSE, TWO READINGS.` · then, large: `A FIFTH OF THE SURPLUS.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn about khums, by sitting with its question. The question isn't how much do I have. It's how much did this year not need. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the last year. What did it actually cost to live it? Then, what came that you didn't need to spend? Don't calculate. Just let the two pictures sit side by side: what the year needed, and what was extra. Notice how the second one looks. The bell holds the time.
Khums. A fifth. From Qur'an eight forty-one: in Sunni law, on spoils and found treasure; in Twelver Shia law, also on the year's surplus. Today's word.

Your line: a fifth of the surplus. Today, if you know someone who keeps khums, or someone who doesn't, ask them how they think about it, and listen. Tomorrow: with dignity. Day one thousand one hundred one.

howItsDone: Twelver Shia Muslims set a yearly khums date, calculate a fifth of the surplus left after the year's expenses, and pay it through the office of the marja' they follow; Sunni Muslims apply a fifth to found treasure and pay zakat on their savings.
